title: The First Declension
subtitle: puella, puella, puellam, puellae, puellae, puellā.
objectives: Decline any first-declension noun in all six cases, both numbers.
Recognize first-declension endings by sight and sound.
Translate simple sentences using first-declension nouns as subjects and objects.
Understand the function of each case without English prepositions.

sections.heading: What is a declension
sections.body:
Latin nouns change their endings to show their function in the sentence. A noun can be a subject, an object, a possessor, a recipient, or several other roles. In English we signal these functions with word order and prepositions: 'the girl sees the woman' vs. 'the woman sees the girl'. In Latin we signal them with case endings.

The first declension contains mostly feminine nouns ending in -a. The model noun is puella (girl). There are five cases you will use constantly, plus a sixth (the vocative) used for direct address. Here is the full paradigm:

          Singular    Plural
  Nom.    puella      puellae
  Gen.    puellae     puellārum
  Dat.    puellae     puellīs
  Acc.    puellam     puellās
  Abl.    puellā      puellīs
  Voc.    puella      puellae

The nominative is the subject. The accusative is the direct object. The genitive shows possession. The dative is the indirect object. The ablative does everything else (means, manner, place, time, agent). The vocative is for calling someone directly.

sections.heading: Examples from Vergil and Ovid
sections.body:
puella in viā est. — The girl is in the street. (nominative subject)
puellam videō. — I see the girl. (accusative object)
vīta puellae brevis est. — The life of the girl is short. (genitive possessive)
puellae rosam dō. — I give a rose to the girl. (dative indirect object)
cum puellā ambulō. — I walk with the girl. (ablative of accompaniment)
puella, venī! — Girl, come! (vocative direct address)

Ovid writes: forma bonum fragile est. — Beauty is a fragile good. 'forma' is nominative singular, subject of 'est'.

Vergil writes: Trōiae ā lītoribus ad Italiam vēnērunt. — They came from the shores of Troy to Italy. 'Trōiae' is genitive singular, modifying 'lītoribus'.

sections.heading: Paradigm table
sections.body:
Memorize the endings, not the translations. The endings are the grammar; the translations are just glosses.

          Singular    Plural
  Nom.    -a          -ae
  Gen.    -ae         -ārum
  Dat.    -ae         -īs
  Acc.    -am         -ās
  Abl.    -ā          -īs
  Voc.    -a          -ae
